verses.1: Al-Mizan identifies the pronoun with the whole Qur’an. Inzāl signifies its sudden descent at once, unlike gradual tanzīl, so the commentary affirms a single comprehensive descent to the Prophet alongside the twenty-three-year gradual revelation, and rejects the view that this only marks the first onset of some verses. With (2:185), the verse locates the Night of Destiny in Ramadan, though its precise date requires narrations. Qadr apparently means taqdīr, God’s ordainment of the coming year’s births, deaths, sustenance, felicity, and wretchedness. The present-tense differentiation of matters in (44:4), the night’s superiority to a thousand months, and the angels’ descent support its annual recurrence in Ramadan, even if the Qur’an’s total descent could have occurred on one occasion. Al-Mizan finds no basis for theories that the night occurred only once, ceased after the Prophet, moved between months, or that qadr here means status or constriction. A change in what is decreed (muqaddar) does not change the decree (taqdīr), for events may change in time while fixed in the Guarded Tablet; possible stages of assigning and finalizing affairs are conceivable, but the narrations do not support them.
verses.2: Al-Mizan reads the question as marking the Night of Destiny’s exalted rank. Repeating its name here and in the following verse, rather than replacing it with a pronoun, intensifies that emphasis.
verses.3: Al-Mizan calls the verse a concise explanation of the Night of Destiny’s lofty rank. It reports that exegetes connect its superiority to the excellence of worship then: keeping vigil in worship is better than worship for a thousand months, fitting the Qur’an’s aim of drawing people near to God and the description of the night as blessed (44:3).
verses.4: Al-Mizan notes that tanazzalu was originally tatanazzalu, takes the Spirit apparently as the reality connected with the divine command, and defines idhn as permission that removes impediment. It settles on two readings of min according to amr: if amr is God’s creative command, the angels and Spirit descend by their Lord’s leave from, or because of, that command; if it denotes all events in existence, min has the purposive force of lām, and they descend to manage every affair of creation.
verses.5: Al-Mizan defines salām and salāmah as freedom from outward and inward defects and afflictions. The night’s peace is God’s grace and mercy spreading over worshipers who turn to Him, with the gates of new punishment and misery closed; reports that devils are prevented from their plots follow from this. The alternative that angels greet worshiping believers with peace ultimately returns to the same meaning. These final two verses explain why the night is better than a thousand months.
